deep.reconstruction:
PROBLEM (Aufgabe). Arrange five reversals ('Commutationen') of a galvanic current so that two magnetic needles in the same circuit afterwards swing with the same amplitude as before. This is the setting of the Gauss–Weber multiplier/galvanometer and telegraph work of the 1830s. The previous page carries Gauss's electrodynamic force law dated Aug. 23, so the context is about 1835.

MODEL (implicit; the reconstruction of the model is mine). Each needle is treated as an undamped harmonic oscillator x'' = -w^2 (x - c(t)). Here c(t) is the rest position, which jumps from +a to -a or back at each reversal. The writer's 'Schwingungszeit' 180°/n is the half-period, so n is the angular frequency in degrees per unit time.

Put W = (x - c) + i x'/w. Between jumps, W e^{iwt} is constant. A jump Dc_k at time tau_k changes W e^{iwt} by -Dc_k e^{iw tau_k}. The jumps alternate in sign (-2a, +2a, -2a, +2a, -2a). The oscillation about the current rest position is therefore unchanged in both amplitude and phase iff
  sum_k (-1)^k e^{i n tau_k} = 0.

CONDITIONS. Take the instants tau = T-t, T-u, T, T+u', T+t' and factor out e^{inT}. The condition becomes
  e^{-int} - e^{-inu} + 1 - e^{inu'} + e^{int'} = 0.
Splitting into real and imaginary parts gives
  (1) cos nt - cos nu + 1 - cos nu' + cos nt' = 0
  (2) sin nt - sin nu + 0 + sin nu' - sin nt' = 0
The '.' in the middle column stands for sin 0 = 0. The same two equations with n' give (3) and (4) for the second needle.

SYMMETRIC ANSATZ. Setting u' = u and t' = t satisfies (2) and (4) identically. Equations (1) and (3) then reduce to 2cos nt - 2cos nu + 1 = 0, that is:
  cos nu - cos nt = 1/2
  cos n'u - cos n't = 1/2
This is two transcendental equations in two unknowns, solved 'durch Versuche' (trial and error).

NUMERICAL CASE. The half-periods are 20.6 s and 43.1 s, so n = 180/20.6 = 8.738 °/s and n' = 180/43.1 = 4.176 °/s. The page gives t = 21.00 s and u = 13.72 s.
- First needle: nu = 119.88°, nt = 183.50°, so cos nu - cos nt = -0.4983 + 0.9981 = 0.4999.
- Second needle: n'u = 57.30°, n't = 87.70°, so 0.5403 - 0.0401 = 0.5002.

TIMETABLE. Starting from the first reversal, the commutations fall at 0, t-u = 7.28, t = 21.00, t+u = 34.72, 2t = 42.00 s.

The second column (0, 18.2, 52.5, 86.8, 105) is the first column multiplied by 2.5. This is almost certainly a conversion into beats of a chronometer beating 0.4 s, i.e. 150 beats per minute (my interpretation).

The pencil signature at the bottom reads like 'W. Weber'. It is possibly an archival attribution of the page or of the problem to Wilhelm Weber.
errors: Derivation of conditions (1)-(4) from the undamped oscillator model is correct.
The ansatz u'=u, t'=t is a sufficient special choice, not the general solution. The page does not claim otherwise.
Numerical values t=21.00, u=13.72 satisfy both equations to about 2e-4. A Newton refinement gives roughly t≈20.997, u≈13.719, consistent with the stated precision.
The commutation times 7.28, 21.00, 34.72, 42.00 are correct, as is the factor-2.5 second column.
Implicit physical idealizations: no damping, instantaneous reversals, and a constant deflecting force proportional to current. These are reasonable for the period.

results.what: Condition for a sequence of current reversals to leave a harmonic oscillator's free oscillation unchanged: sum of (-1)^k e^{i n tau_k} = 0, written as cosine and sine equations.
results.modern_name: Step-response superposition / phasor (Duhamel) analysis of a piecewise-constant forced harmonic oscillator; a bang-bang sequence with zero net residual excitation (cf. input shaping)
results.usually_credited_to: Commutation techniques with galvanometer needles are associated with Gauss and W. Weber, 1830s-1840s (e.g. Weber's Zurückwerfungsmethode)

results.what: Symmetric five-reversal schedule T∓t, T∓u, T reducing the problem to cos nu - cos nt = 1/2 for two frequencies simultaneously, solved numerically for half-periods 20.6 s and 43.1 s.
results.modern_name: Symmetric pulse-sequence design for simultaneous cancellation at two frequencies
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss–Weber circle (experimental practice); no specific later credit known

deep.surprise_reason: This is a neat but elementary piece of experimental planning from the Gauss–Weber electromagnetic work, consistent with their known practice. The page may even be in Weber's hand or of Weber's design, given the pencil 'W. Weber'. Nothing here anticipates a later named result.

checkable.asserts: First needle (half-period 20.6 s): cos(nu)-cos(nt)=1/2 holds to ~1e-4
Second needle (half-period 43.1 s): cos(n'u)-cos(n't)=1/2 holds to ~2e-4
With u'=u, t'=t the sine conditions vanish identically (result 0)
The symmetric cosine condition reduces to cos nu - cos nt = 1/2 (result 0)

checkable.sympy: n,T,t,u,u2,t2=symbols('n T t u u2 t2',real=True); expand(exp(-I*n*T)*(exp(I*n*(T-t))-exp(I*n*(T-u))+exp(I*n*T)-exp(I*n*(T+u2))+exp(I*n*(T+t2))),complex=True)
checkable.asserts: Real part is cos nt - cos nu + 1 - cos nu' + cos nt'. Imaginary part is minus the page's sine condition, so both vanish together.
Second column 0, 18.2, 52.5, 86.8, 105 is the first column times 2.5 (chronometer beats of 0.4 s)

transcription_corrections: In the second and fourth equations, the isolated '.' (and the '+ .' in line 2) marks the empty middle term sin(0)=0. It is a placeholder, not punctuation.
'Es seien' is written as one run-together word 'Essein' in the manuscript.
Second column entry '18''2[?]' should read 18.2: the column is consistently the first column times 2.5, i.e. 0, 18.2, 52.5, 86.8, 105.
In the first equation the sign before 'cos nu' is overwritten by an ink blot but must be '-' (consistent with the derivation).
The pencil signature at the bottom plausibly reads 'W. Weber'. It is a later or archival pencil note, not part of the ink text.
